lines.text: An island with no people at all, home to a bird that would vanish, then a meeting place of Europe, Africa and India. This is the story of Mauritius.
For millions of years a large, flightless bird lived here, the dodo. Soon after sailors arrived it was gone, and it became the symbol of extinction.
The Dutch had named the island Mauritius, and in 1638 they settled it, though they left again by 1710.
In 1715 France took over and renamed it Isle de France, a base for its ships in the Indian Ocean.
In 1735 the French governor Mahe de La Bourdonnais founded Port Louis, today the capital.
In 1810 the French beat the British navy at Grand Port, their only naval victory over Britain in the Napoleonic Wars. That same year, Britain took the island anyway.
After slavery ended, workers were brought from India. Some half a million indentured labourers landed at the depot of Aapravasi Ghat.
Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, a doctor, would lead the island to freedom and become the father of the nation.
His son Navin would follow him as prime minister, and return to the post again in 2024.
In 1968 Mauritius became independent from Britain, and grew into one of the richest and most stable democracies in Africa.
In 2008 Le Morne, the mountain where runaway slaves once hid, was listed as a World Heritage Site, so their story would not be forgotten.
From the lost dodo to a thriving democracy, Mauritius made a nation from many peoples.
